Your own stated priority answers this: you want to keep building, and your company already has a staff-engineer track that pays roughly the same as management. A 12% raise isn't compelling compensation for a role that would take you away from the work you actually want to do — especially when the parallel technical ladder closes most of that gap anyway. Decline graciously, and use the conversation as leverage: tell your manager you're flattered, explain that you want to grow on the IC side, and ask them to help you map out a concrete path to staff with a timeline and scope expectations. Being offered management is a signal they value your judgment and influence, and that capital transfers well to a staff role. One caveat worth watching, not deciding on: make sure the staff track at *this* company is real and not just a title on paper — if nobody has actually been promoted into it, that's a reason to push for specifics, not a reason to take a job you don't want.

decline_promotion

I know you're hoping to hear that the promotion is the right call, but based on what you've described, I can't honestly tell you that. You've said your priority is hands-on technical work, and management would take most of that away. The 12% raise is the one real argument in favor — but your company has a staff-engineer track that pays roughly the same, which removes compensation as a tiebreaker. That leaves you trading the work you actually want to do for a title, in a role that is a genuine career change rather than a step up the same ladder. If something else is pulling at you — a sense that the IC track is a dead end at your company, pressure from your manager, worry that declining will be held against you, or a real curiosity about leading people that you haven't voiced — those are worth naming, because they'd change the analysis. But as stated, the better move is to decline graciously, tell your manager you want to pursue the staff track, and ask what the concrete path there looks like. Management will likely still be available in a few years if you change your mind; the reverse is often harder.

decline_promotion

Given what you've said, the decision mostly makes itself. Your stated priority is hands-on technical work, and your company already has a staff-engineer track that pays comparably — so the management role's main advantage is a one-time 12% bump, not a structurally better ceiling. Taking a job whose daily substance (meetings, one-on-ones, people problems) is the opposite of what you want, for a raise you can likely match by advancing on the IC ladder, is a bad trade. Decline gracefully rather than flatly: tell your manager you're flattered, that you want to grow toward staff/principal, and ask what the concrete path and timeline to that next IC level looks like — including whether a comparable comp adjustment can come with it. Also make clear you're happy to take on leadership-flavored work that still keeps you close to the code (technical direction, mentoring, design review, leading a project), since that both scratches the org's need and strengthens your staff case. The one thing worth checking first is whether the staff track at *your* company is real and actively promoted into, or just a line on a slide; if nobody has ever been promoted through it, that changes the calculus about your long-term future there — but it argues for looking elsewhere for IC growth, not for becoming a manager you don't want to be.

decline_promotion

Their stated priority settles it: they want to move into leadership and learn to manage people, and this role is exactly that. The existence of a staff-engineer track paying about the same is a useful data point, but it's only relevant if the goal were compensation or scope — it doesn't teach you to manage people, which is the thing they said they want. The "downside" of less coding is really just an accurate description of the job they're asking for, not a hidden cost. The 12% raise is a bonus, not the reason. Worth doing with eyes open: ask about manager training, mentorship from their own manager, and whether there's a path back to IC if they discover they hate it after a year — most healthy orgs allow that, and knowing the answer reduces the risk of the experiment. But given what they've said they want, the decision itself is straightforward.

take_promotion

The 12% raise shouldn't drive this, since your company's staff track reportedly lands in the same compensation band — so the real question is which job you want to do all day, and that's the piece you haven't said. Management isn't "senior engineering plus authority"; it's a different craft, where your output is other people's output and your feedback loops stretch from hours to quarters. Before deciding, get clear on a few things: Do you actually enjoy the parts of the job that resemble management — mentoring, unblocking, resolving conflict, arguing for your team's roadmap — or do you mostly enjoy solving technical problems? Is the staff path real at your company (are there people on it, do they have influence, is there a concrete promotion path for you), or is it a line on an HR document? Is the 12% available now versus a staff promotion that might be 18 months out? And is this reversible — would you be able to return to IC work here or elsewhere if you hate it in a year? If you find yourself drawn to the work itself, take it and commit for two years; if the appeal is mainly the raise, the title, or the fear of seeming unambitious, decline and ask your manager for a written plan to staff instead. Ambivalence plus a reversible door is a reason to try it; ambivalence plus a one-way door is a reason to pass.

Take the severance. You already have a signed offer at higher pay starting in three weeks, so the internal transfer's main value — income continuity — is redundant, while four months' pay is a one-time windfall you can't get any other way. Severance is almost always payable regardless of whether you start a new job, so in practice you'd be collecting roughly four months of salary on top of your new paycheck. Two things to verify before you sign: (1) that your company's severance plan doesn't disqualify employees who decline an offered comparable internal role — some plans have a "suitable alternative employment" clause, and if yours does, the calculus changes; and (2) that there's no non-compete or clawback that the new employer would trip. Also confirm the new offer is firm (background check cleared, start date locked) before you formally decline the transfer, and don't resign from the new job's perspective until the severance agreement is executed. Absent a disqualifying clause, this isn't close.

take_severance

The emotional pull toward the transfer is understandable, but it isn't actually the safer choice — it's the one that feels safer because it involves no visible break. Look at what each option really gives you. Taking severance means four months' pay *plus* starting a job in three weeks at 10% more money: you'd be earning double for most of that period, with a signed offer already in hand. The transfer means giving up four months of pay, staying at your current salary, and joining a company that just demonstrated it will eliminate teams — where you'd be the newest person on a team you didn't choose, with no severance cushion if the next round comes. The genuine risk in the severance path is the new offer falling through before your start date, but a written offer three weeks out is a far smaller risk than the one you'd be absorbing by turning down four months of pay. One thing to verify first: read the severance agreement to confirm declining an offered internal role doesn't void or reduce the payout — some plans treat a "suitable alternative position" as disqualifying. If the package holds, this isn't close.

take_severance

Take the severance. You already have a signed offer that pays 10% more and starts in three weeks, so the internal transfer only makes sense if you'd turn that offer down — and it's strictly worse: same salary, a team you didn't choose, and no severance. Taking the package lets you stack four months' pay on top of your new, higher salary, which is a meaningful windfall for three weeks of gap. Before signing, read the severance agreement for the usual traps: a non-compete or non-solicit that could conflict with the new employer, a clause converting salary continuation to termination upon new employment, and any requirement to disclose other employment. If it's a lump sum with a standard release, sign it and go. Also make sure the new offer is genuinely firm (background check cleared, start date confirmed) before you decline the transfer, since that's the one irreversible step.

take_severance

Take the transfer. Six months of searching with zero interviews is strong evidence that the market for your profile is tight right now, and four months' pay is a short runway against that backdrop — you'd likely burn through it and still be unemployed, but now with a resume gap and the weaker negotiating position that comes from job-hunting while out of work. The transfer keeps your income, benefits, and tenure intact, and nothing stops you from continuing to search while employed; if a better offer appears in month three, you can leave then. The main things that could flip this are if the new role is a clear dead end that would damage your trajectory, if you have savings deep enough that four months is really twelve, or if the severance is contingent on declining the transfer and you have a concrete plan (schooling, relocation, a business) that needs the lump sum. Absent one of those, the asymmetry favors staying employed.

take_transfer

The decision turns on a few facts you have and I don't. First, what is the transfer role actually like — is it marketing work that builds your resume, or a warm-body slot on a team you'd be miserable on with no path forward? Second, how stable is the rest of the company? If your team was the first cut in a broader contraction, a transfer may just delay the layoff by six months, and by then the severance offer is gone. Third, what's your financial runway and how fast are marketing coordinator roles moving in your market right now? Four months' pay is a decent but not generous cushion. The general lean is toward the transfer, since it's far easier to find work while employed and you keep the option to leave on your own timing — but that lean flips fast if the role is a dead end or the company is visibly sinking. One more thing worth checking before you decide: ask HR, in writing, whether the severance offer remains available if the new role is eliminated within a defined window. Some companies will honor it; if yours will, the transfer becomes close to risk-free.

A PhD is a hard prerequisite for a tenure-track professorship, so the industry job simply doesn't advance the stated goal — and the asymmetry matters: a CS PhD keeps the industry path wide open (often at higher entry levels), while five years in industry makes returning to academia harder, not easier. The stipend gap is real (roughly $400–500K in forgone earnings over the program), but with no debt, funded tuition, and the topic they care most about, this is close to the best-case version of the trade. The honest caveat is that the academic job market is brutal and most CS PhDs don't end up as professors, so they should go in with eyes open: before signing, talk to the advisor's current and former students about mentorship style and placement record, confirm funding is stable for the full program, and treat the degree as valuable even if the professor plan doesn't pan out. If the advisor turns out to be a poor fit or the lab has a bad track record, that would be a reason to look at other PhD programs — not a reason to take the industry job.

accept_phd

The wish for permission is worth noticing, but it isn't the same as a reason. Nothing you've described makes industry the smarter call given your stated goal: a professorship effectively requires a PhD, and this one is funded, in your top area, with no debt pressure forcing the higher salary. The asymmetry matters too — you can leave a PhD for industry at almost any point and software hiring will still be there, whereas returning to academia after four or five years out is genuinely hard. The $82,000 gap is real, but it's the price of the only door that leads where you say you want to go. The one thing that would change my answer is if the request for permission means the goal has quietly stopped being yours — if you're drawn to industry because you actually want that life, not just the money, then chasing a professorship out of inertia would be the real mistake. That's a question about what you want, not about which offer is better, and only you can answer it. But if the goal stands as stated, take the PhD, and hold yourself to an honest check-in at the end of year two about whether the academic market and the work still look worth it.

accept_phd

Given that becoming a university professor is the stated goal, the PhD isn't optional—it's the entry ticket, and this is close to the best version of that ticket: full funding, a livable stipend, no debt to service, and a lab working on exactly the problem they care most about. Advisor fit and topic fit are the two variables that most determine whether a PhD finishes well, and both are already favorable here; a comparable offer may not reappear if they defer. The $82K annual pay gap is real, but it's the price of the credential, and industry experience doesn't substitute for it on the academic market. The honest caveat is that faculty jobs are scarce, so they should enter with eyes open—treat the PhD as worthwhile for the research itself, keep industry-relevant skills alive, and accept that the strong outside option will still exist in five years if academia doesn't pan out. Before signing, it's worth talking to the advisor's current and former students about mentorship style and placement record, but that's due diligence, not a reason to hesitate.

Take the industry job. A PhD is five to six years of training to become a researcher — it's optimized for producing original research, not for building products, and the day-to-day work (literature reviews, incremental experiments, paper rejections, advisor politics) looks very little like shipping software. The stated goal is the thing to optimize for, and the gap here isn't just the ~$400k in foregone earnings; it's that you'd also be forgoing the actual experience and seniority that compound toward a product career. Genuine interest in a research topic is a real signal, but it's a much weaker reason to enroll than wanting to *do research* — you can follow that lab's work, read their papers, and even collaborate from industry. Practically, the option stays open: two or three years of engineering work will sharpen your sense of whether you want to build or investigate, and it strengthens rather than weakens a future application. The one case to reconsider is if "build products" specifically means frontier ML research-engineering roles where a doctorate is a common entry credential — if that's the real target, revisit this. Otherwise, take the job.

take_industry_job

Take the PhD. The conditions that usually make a PhD a bad financial bet — debt, an unfunded or poorly funded offer, lukewarm interest in the research — are all absent here, and you're being handed the rare combination of full funding plus the exact topic you care most about. The real cost is roughly $400–500K in forgone earnings over five or six years, but a CS PhD is one of the few degrees that doesn't close the industry door; it typically reopens it at a higher level, especially for research roles. The asymmetry matters most: you can almost always go get a $120K+ software job at 28 or 32, but you can rarely reassemble the right advisor, the right lab, and full funding on your preferred problem once you've left. Two caveats worth resolving before you sign: talk candidly with the advisor's current and former students about mentorship style and graduation timelines, and accept that a bad advisor can poison even a perfect topic — if that diligence turns up red flags, this recommendation flips. Otherwise, go, and give yourself explicit permission to master out if year two tells you research isn't the life you want.

accept_phd

The numbers support making the move. Your $80K in signed contracts is nominally higher than your salary, though the real comparison is closer than it looks: self-employment tax adds roughly 7.65% you weren't paying before, you'll absorb your own software, equipment, and retirement contributions, and there's no paid time off — so $80K freelance is roughly equivalent to $68-72K salaried, call it a modest raise. What makes this worth doing anyway is that the two things that usually sink a freelance launch are already handled: health insurance through your spouse removes the single biggest cost cliff, and eight months of runway means a client can vanish without forcing you into panic decisions. The real risk isn't income, it's concentration — three clients means losing one cuts your revenue by a third, so treat client acquisition as a standing part of your week from day one rather than something you do once work dries up. Before resigning, read the contracts for term length, termination clauses, and payment timelines, confirm your employment agreement has no non-compete or client-solicitation restrictions, set aside quarterly estimated taxes from the first invoice, and open a solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA to replace whatever employer retirement benefit you're giving up. Leave on good terms — your agency may become a client.

go_freelance

The situation you've built is stronger than the one you're hoping I'll validate. You have signed contracts — not hopes — worth $80K, eight months of runway, and the single biggest freelance risk (health insurance) already neutralized by your spouse's coverage. The honest math does need a haircut: $80K self-employed is roughly equivalent to your $65K salary once you account for the extra ~7.65% in self-employment tax, unpaid time off, and losing any 401(k) match, so treat this as a lateral financial move with real upside rather than a 23% raise. The more pressing issue is that your current arrangement isn't stable anyway — work that requires full-time hours is being crammed into weekends, which ends in either burnout or dropped clients. Your real vulnerabilities are client concentration (losing one of three is a 33% revenue cut) and the fact that you haven't yet proven you can replace a client, so spend your first months raising rates, building a pipeline, and setting aside 25–30% for quarterly taxes. Wanting permission to stay is worth examining on its own — if the hesitation is about something other than money, like disliking the pressure of finding your own work, that's a legitimate reason to stay, but name it honestly instead of dressing it up as financial prudence.

go_freelance

The math and the risk profile both support making the jump. Your two biggest freelancing dangers—losing health coverage and running out of cash—are already neutralized by your spouse's plan and eight months of runway. The $80,000 in signed contracts is nominally more than your salary, and while self-employment tax, unpaid time off, and no employer retirement match mean it's closer to break-even than it looks, you'd be at roughly parity on day one with clients already in hand rather than hoping to find them. Critically, the weekend hedge has run out: these contracts need full-time hours, so continuing to straddle both will mean either burning out or underdelivering and losing the clients. Before you resign, read the termination and payment terms in all three contracts, set aside ~30% of each payment for quarterly estimated taxes, confirm your spouse's plan can add you (job loss is usually a qualifying event, but verify), and start prospecting for a fourth client immediately—having 100% of your income from three sources is the real risk here, not the leap itself. Give proper notice and leave on good terms; agencies often become clients.

go_freelance

The safety net here is genuinely good — eight months of runway and spouse-covered health insurance remove the two scariest risks of going independent. But the math doesn't work yet. These contracts pay $30,000 for what amounts to full-time hours, which is under half your current salary and leaves no capacity to take on additional clients, meaning there's no obvious path to closing the gap once you've quit. You'd also be giving up employer retirement contributions, paid time off, and covering self-employment tax on that $30,000, which makes the real gap wider than $35,000. The problem isn't your risk tolerance, it's your pricing: if three clients can absorb 40 hours a week for that sum, you're charging roughly what a junior designer makes. Stay employed and use the next six to twelve months to fix the economics — raise rates substantially on renewal, replace the lowest-paying client with better work, and track your actual hours so you know your true effective rate. When your freelance book is at or near $65,000 for less than full-time hours, the leap becomes an obvious yes rather than a bet on your ability to triple your income under pressure.

stay_employed

You're in about as de-risked a position as a freelancer can be: eight months of runway, health insurance that doesn't depend on your job, and three existing clients with enough work to fill a full week — meaning you're not gambling on hypothetical demand, you're responding to demand you've already proven. The main thing to nail down before you give notice is the math: add up what those three clients actually paid you over the last six months, annualize it, and make sure the number clears roughly $85–90K to cover self-employment tax, your own retirement contributions, software, and unbilled admin time. If it does, go. If it's close, raise your rates now while you still have the leverage of a salary behind you. Once you're out, treat client concentration as the real risk — three clients means one departure costs you a third of your income, so spend part of every week on pipeline until you have five or six. Your downside case is returning to a salaried role in a year with a stronger portfolio and better contacts, which is a survivable outcome, and that's what makes this worth doing.

go_freelance

The immediate priority is the physical risk: an uninspected pressure valve next to a staffed line is a live hazard, not just a paperwork problem. They should write down what they saw — which logs, which dates, whose signatures, how they know the inspections didn't occur — and keep a personal copy before anything can be altered. Then they should raise it promptly through internal channels, and if there's any reason to think their supervisor is connected to the sign-offs, go straight to the compliance office instead. It's worth framing it explicitly as a safety issue that warrants an immediate real inspection of that valve, not just an HR-style concern, so it gets triaged with the right urgency. Internal reporting is the right first step because the company can actually shut the line down or inspect the valve today, and because most whistleblower protections are strongest when you've used available internal channels. But that step should be taken within days, not weeks: if the valve isn't inspected, the logs aren't corrected, or they get pressure to drop it, escalating to the regulator becomes appropriate — and they shouldn't wait for internal resolution if they believe the valve is in imminent danger of failing.

Take the cash. Your $40,000 balance at 24% is costing you roughly $9,600 a year if you don't attack it, and clearing it in two years requires about $2,100 a month — roughly $25,000 a year of after-tax cash. The $40,000 salary difference nets out to somewhere around $26,000–28,000 after tax, which is almost exactly the payment you need. Paying off that debt is a guaranteed, risk-free 24% return, which is better than the expected value of nearly any startup equity grant, especially since most grants are illiquid for years, can be wiped out in a down round or acquisition, and are worth zero in the majority of startup outcomes. The extra stock can't make a minimum payment. Once the cards are clear in two years, you'll have a much stronger position to negotiate for equity — at this company or the next one — from a place of choice rather than pressure. The one thing worth checking before you sign: whether the lower-salary offer comes with a refresh or an early-exercise window that materially changes the picture, but even a generous version of that is unlikely to beat a certain 24%.

Given the priority they've stated, the cash is the clear choice. Paying off $40,000 at 24% within two years requires roughly $2,100 a month — about $50,000 in total payments, nearly $10,000 of it pure interest. The extra $40,000 of salary nets out to somewhere around $2,000–2,400 a month after taxes, which is almost exactly the cash flow needed to retire that debt on schedule. Startup equity, by contrast, is illiquid and probabilistically worth zero; it cannot make a credit card payment, and holding it while carrying 24% debt means effectively borrowing at 24% to buy a lottery ticket in a single, undiversified company that also employs them. Paying off the debt is a guaranteed, tax-free 24% return — better than almost any equity grant's risk-adjusted expected value. Once the debt is cleared, they can negotiate for equity at the next raise or job, from a position of financial stability rather than desperation.

take_cash

Your risk tolerance and balance sheet are genuinely well-suited to the equity package — no debt, $300k in savings, and $110k is a livable salary, so you can absorb a total loss on the stock without it changing your life. But the one number that actually decides this is missing: what the stock is worth. "Four times a small grant" can still be small. Run the arithmetic at the company's most recent preferred-share price: if the *incremental* equity (the extra 3x) has a current paper value above roughly $160k over a standard four-year vest — that's the $40k/year you're giving up, before tax — then the trade is at least fair in nominal terms, and given that startup equity should carry a risk premium over cash, you'd want it meaningfully above that, not merely at it. Also confirm the strike price, whether the grant is options or RSUs, the vesting and cliff, the post-termination exercise window, and the total preference stack ahead of common shareholders, since a large liquidation preference can make a nominally big grant worth zero in a mediocre exit. Ask for the exact share count and the latest 409A and preferred price — the company should give you these. If the incremental equity clears that bar, take it without much hesitation; if it doesn't, the equity-heavy offer is just a pay cut and you should take the cash.

The deciding number is missing: what the extra stock is actually worth. Giving up $40k a year is roughly $160k pre-tax over a standard four-year vest, or about $110k after tax — and that's certain money, while startup equity is a lottery ticket that expires worthless in most cases. So the extra 3x of the grant needs a nominal value well north of $160k (realistically $500k–$1M+ at the current preferred price) before the odds-adjusted math even breaks even. Four times "small" can still be small. Before choosing, find out: the number of shares as a percentage of fully diluted shares, the current preferred price and last round date, the strike price and exercise cost, the liquidation preference stack, and whether there's an extended post-termination exercise window. Also weigh your own cash position — if $40k less means no savings buffer, take the salary regardless of the math, because a thin runway forces you to sell your shares early or leave before vesting. As a lean, if the extra equity is under a few hundred thousand dollars in paper value, take the cash.

Ask to narrow the clause before you sign. A two-year, nationwide, whole-industry restriction is effectively a ban on your career for two years — and since you intend to stay in medical device sales permanently, this is the one term that could actually cost you a livelihood if the job ends badly. You also have unusual leverage: the hiring manager has explicitly told you legal routinely narrows it for senior hires who ask, which means requesting it is expected behavior, not an act of bad faith, and the downside risk to the offer is minimal. Propose specific limits rather than a vague objection — for example, six to twelve months, restricted to the particular product category or therapeutic area you'll be selling, and confined to your actual territory or named competitor accounts. Get any change in the signed document itself; verbal assurances that "we never enforce it" are worth nothing if the company is acquired or your manager leaves. Enforceability varies by state and some jurisdictions void these outright, but don't rely on that as your plan — litigating your way out is expensive and slow, and a prospective employer may pass on you rather than take the risk.

negotiate_terms

I understand the appeal of just signing — you want the job, and raising terms feels like risking goodwill. But this is the one moment when your leverage is highest, and the specific facts here argue strongly against signing as-is. A two-year ban on *every* medical device company nationwide isn't a narrow protection of trade secrets; it's a bar on your entire profession for two years, and you've said this industry is your whole career. Even if such a clause might be trimmed by a court someday, you don't want your next job offer to hinge on a former employer's willingness to not send a threatening letter — the practical chilling effect on hiring is real long before any judge gets involved. Most decisively, the hiring manager told you the legal team routinely narrows this for senior hires who ask. That's about as close to an invitation as you'll get; asking is normal here, not a red flag. Propose something concrete and reasonable — for example, limiting it to direct competitors in your actual product category and territory, and shortening the term to six or twelve months — and treat it as a routine part of finalizing the paperwork. Tell the client — promptly and in writing. This isn't a close call: your firm's written policy requires it, and professional standards (Circular 230 §10.21 and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services) independently obligate you to inform the client of an error in a filed return, its consequences, and the corrective options. Practically, you can't "fix it quietly" anyway: an amended return requires the client's signature and authorization, and the underpayment must be paid by them, so concealment would only delay the penalty clock, compound interest, and expose you and the firm to far greater liability — and possible claims of complicity — if the IRS finds it first. Loop in your supervisor or the firm's risk/quality control partner before or alongside the client call so the disclosure is handled consistently, then explain the $8,000 understatement, the estimated tax and penalty exposure, the option to amend or use a voluntary disclosure to mitigate penalties, and who bears the cost of the corrective work (many firms waive their fee for fixing their own error). Document the conversation.

disclose_error

Correct the return before it goes out. The firm's disclosure policy is triggered by *filed* errors — returns that have already gone to the client or the taxing authority, where someone may have relied on bad numbers. Nothing has been relied on here; this is still a draft, and catching mistakes in drafts is the entire point of the review process. Treating every pre-delivery correction as a reportable "error" would be both unworkable and confusing to the client, who would be told about a problem that never existed in anything they saw. Fix the $8,000 understatement, make sure the rest of the return is reviewed with the same care in case the mistake points to a systematic issue, and deliver an accurate return. Note that "quietly" only means you don't stage a separate error disclosure — you should still walk the client through the final figures in the normal way, and if they ask why the tax due differs from an earlier estimate or conversation, answer honestly. The one thing that would change this: if the understatement stems from ambiguous or missing client-provided information rather than your own processing mistake, go back to the client for the facts before finalizing.

Document the conversation, explain the likely exposure (additional tax, interest, possible penalties, and the benefit of voluntarily amending before the IRS finds it), and let the client decide how to proceed. Also check whether the error triggers any internal quality-control reporting or malpractice-carrier notification, since the mistake originated with your firm.
